Q: FillRect disappears after some time A:

Thanks to @HansPassant and @Igor Tandetnik it was solved. As @3CEZVQ stated the issue was that i was creating too many brushes. I needed to call CreateSolidBrush once in WM_CREATE and then delete it after elsewhere.

Q: Disable font-lock-warning-face in Emacs A:

This is interesting. font-lock-warning-face is applied by modes during font-locking. Remapping via face-remapping-alist is buffer-local and non-invasive. You dont need to redefine the face. You just tell Emacs to display it as another face. Remapping to default makes the text appear normal, which matches “make the face be not applied.”

Add to init.el

;;; Disable application of font-lock-warning-face everywhere by remapping it
(defun rd/disable-font-lock-warning-face ()
  "Remap `font-lock-warning-face` to `default` in the current buffer."
  (setq-local face-remapping-alist
              (cons '(font-lock-warning-face default)
                    (assq-delete-all 'font-lock-warning-face face-remapping-alist))))
(add-hook 'after-change-major-mode-hook #'rd/disable-font-lock-warning-face)
(add-hook 'change-major-mode-after-body-hook #'rd/disable-font-lock-warning-face)

If you want this only for certain modes like all prog-mode descendants, then swap the hook - (add-hook 'prog-mode-hook #'rd/disable-font-lock-warning-face)

Updating the answer based on the comments

Many modes attach font-lock-warning-face via font-lock-keywords. Remapping doesn’t fight that at all, rather, it simply tells Emacs to display anything with that face as if it were default. Because default has no special overriding attributes, your custom faces (like keyword/constant/string faces from your theme) can still apply and be visible. This is buffer-local, reversible, and doesn’t mutate the face definition or each mode’s font-lock rules.

You can add this to your init.el then:

;;; Disable application of font-lock-warning-face everywhere by remapping it
(defun rd/neutralize-font-lock-warning-face ()
  "Make `font-lock-warning-face` effectively inert in the current buffer."
  ;; Remove any prior remapping for idempotency, then add ours.
  (setq-local face-remapping-alist
              (cons '(font-lock-warning-face default)
                    (assq-delete-all 'font-lock-warning-face face-remapping-alist))))

;; Apply to all buffers whenever the major mode changes.
(add-hook 'after-change-major-mode-hook #'rd/neutralize-font-lock-warning-face)
(add-hook 'change-major-mode-after-body-hook #'rd/neutralize-font-lock-warning-face)

;; If you prefer restricting this to programming modes:
;; (add-hook 'prog-mode-hook #'rd/neutralize-font-lock-warning-face)

In cases where you have multiple faces on a region and want to ensure font-lock-warning-face contributes nothing to the merge. Remapping to default already does that for most themes, but if you need to be extra strict, you can remap to a deliberately empty face. This will ensure that when font-lock-warning-face is present alongside your theme’s faces, it contributes no attributes at all.

(defface rd/empty-face
  '((t :inherit nil
       :foreground unspecified
       :background unspecified
       :underline nil
       :weight unspecified
       :slant unspecified))
  "A face with no attributes, used to neutralize other faces."
  :group 'faces)

(defun rd/neutralize-font-lock-warning-face-strict ()
  (setq-local face-remapping-alist
              (cons '(font-lock-warning-face rd/empty-face)
                    (assq-delete-all 'font-lock-warning-face face-remapping-alist))))

(add-hook 'after-change-major-mode-hook #'rd/neutralize-font-lock-warning-face-strict)

Hope it helps.

Q: Why does the repr() of a string have two sets of quotes? And why don't I get the object back when I eval() it? A:

  1. The result of repr('foo') is the string 'foo'. In your Python shell, the result of the expression is expressed as a representation too, so you're essentially seeing repr(repr('foo')).

  2. eval calculates the result of an expression. The result is always a value (such as a number, a string, or an object). Multiple variables can refer to the same value, as in:

     x = 'foo'
 y = x

    x and y now refer to the same value.

  3. I don’t have any idea what you meant here. Can you post an example, and what you'd like to see?

Q: Mix samples using SoX library A:

Using SoX from the command line:

sox --combine mix \
    "|sox sample1.mp3 -p" \
    "|sox sample2.mp3 -p trim 0.3342" \
    "|sox sample3.mp3 -p trim 0.3342 trim 0 0.3442" \
    "|sox sample4.mp3 -p trim 1.2243" \
    "|sox sample1.mp3 -p trim 1.223434 trim 0 1.224244" out.mp3

I'm assuming you mean to take .3442 seconds starting from .3342.

If you mean "stop at .3442 into the original file to get a 0.01 second sample", invert the order of the trims
